overview:
Rome's great amphitheatre rose on ground that had recently been a private lake. Nero's sprawling Golden House had swallowed a swathe of the city centre after the fire of 64, and when Vespasian took power at the end of the civil wars of 69 he began, around 70, to give that land back to the public in the most conspicuous form available: a stone arena for the whole populace, paid for — according to an inscription reconstructed from the peg-holes left in a reused block — out of the spoils of the Jewish War and the sack of Jerusalem. Titus opened it in 80 with games said to have run a hundred days; Domitian appears to have finished the upper storey and the underground service level in the years after, which is roughly where this story's start date of 82 falls. The building was known simply as the amphitheatre, or later the Flavian Amphitheatre; the name Colosseum attached itself only much later, from the colossal bronze statue of Nero that stood beside it.

What went on inside followed a set rhythm: animal hunts in the morning, executions at midday, gladiators in the afternoon, with the arena floor drained, flooded, or dressed as a forest as the programme required. Beneath it ran the hypogeum, a two-storey warren of corridors, cages and hand-cranked lifts that could deliver a beast or a piece of scenery into the daylight on cue. Seating was arranged by rank, so that a spectator's place in the tiers advertised his place in Roman society, and the whole structure — travertine outside, concrete and brick and volcanic tufa within, four storeys of superimposed architectural orders, a retractable awning worked by sailors — was as much an argument about imperial generosity as it was a venue. Estimates of capacity vary widely; ancient figures run to eighty-seven thousand, modern reconstructions usually settle nearer fifty thousand.

Gladiatorial combat faded out in the fifth century and animal shows in the sixth, and thereafter the building simply became part of Rome. Earthquakes in the fifth and sixth centuries, then again in 847, 1231 and above all 1349, brought down much of the outer ring on the south side. What was left served in turn as housing, workshops, a fortress held by the Frangipane and Annibaldi families, and for centuries a quarry whose travertine and iron clamps went into the palaces and churches of the medieval and Renaissance city. Papal protection came in the eighteenth century, partly on the strength of a tradition that Christian martyrs had died there — a belief for which historians find no evidence, and which the medieval pilgrimage guides do not support. Systematic excavation followed in the nineteenth century, and the first full cleaning and repair in the building's history only in the 2010s.
significance: More than any other surviving structure, the Colosseum fixed what a mass venue looks like: an elliptical bowl of tiered seating served by numbered entrances and radial passages, a plan that Roman engineers exported across the empire and that stadium architects still work within. It also stands as the most legible physical record of a Roman political bargain — the emperor buying consent with spectacle, on land reclaimed from a hated predecessor, with money taken from a conquered province. Its long afterlife as fortress, quarry and shrine made it a byword for the passage of empires, quoted by pilgrims and Romantic poets alike, and by the modern era it had become the single image that stands in for ancient Rome itself, protected within the Historic Centre of Rome World Heritage site and named among the New Seven Wonders in 2007.
coverage: Written from the Wikipedia and Britannica entries and the World History Encyclopedia article, cross-checked by search; the dataset itself holds no events beneath this story, so the map can show nothing for it. The building is exceptionally well documented as a structure but thinly documented as an institution: the funding inscription is a modern reconstruction rather than a surviving text, capacity figures are contested by a factor of nearly two, the exact division of work between Titus and Domitian is inferred, and almost nothing survives from the point of view of the people who fought and died in it.
